summary:
Khonsu is a web-based self-assessment health monitor for astronauts on long-duration missions. A crew member logs eight indicators measurable on board: resting heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, body temperature, fasting blood glucose, sleep, mood and exercise. Each reading is compared with a sourced reference range and shown as Nominal, Caution or Act now, together with what to do now, when to re-check and when to escalate to the crew medical officer or to flight surgeons on Earth.
The app is built around NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight (RIDGE). Mission profiles for the ISS, the Moon, Mars transit and Mars surface show the real communication delay, and trend views catch slow changes that a single reading would miss.
Far from Earth, astronauts must notice health changes themselves. Khonsu supports that decision; it does not diagnose or treat.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Khonsu is a self-assessment health monitor for astronauts on long-duration missions. A crew member logs eight indicators that can be measured on board: resting heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, body temperature, fasting blood glucose, sleep, mood and exercise. Mission radiation dose is tracked as well.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Log - readings are entered from on-board devices or self-report.

2. Assess - each value is compared with a sourced reference range and with the crew member's personal baseline. The result is Nominal, Caution, Act now, or Re-measure when a reading is too old.

3. Guide - every non-nominal result comes with what to do now, when to re-check and when to escalate.

4. Escalate - reports go to the crew medical officer or to flight surgeons on Earth, with the real one-way signal delay for the selected mission.

Combination rules raise the level when related values are off together, for example a raised temperature with a raised heart rate.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Spaceflight changes the body slowly and quietly. Khonsu turns a short daily check into an early warning: trend views catch gradual changes that a single reading would miss, and the escalation logic tells the astronaut when self-care is enough and when Earth must be told. The same approach could help people in other isolated places, such as polar stations or ships.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- The whole app is organised around NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight (RIDGE); every indicator is linked to at least one hazard.

- Mission profiles for the ISS, the Moon, Mars transit and Mars surface change the communication delay shown to the crew.

- A crew board shows the status of all crew members at a glance.

- A sleep-shift colour mode with warm, low-blue colours for use before rest.

- A streak counter rewards regular check-ins, not "healthy" answers.

- A Methodology page answers NASA's five challenge questions and lists the source of every threshold.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- The tool supports self-assessment only; it does not diagnose or treat.

- Reference ranges are defined on Earth and are marked as defaults pending science review.

- All readings shown in the demo are synthetic.

- Accessibility: status is always given in words as well as colour.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Languages: TypeScript (all app code), CSS (Tailwind CSS v4), HTML; JavaScript (Node.js) for the 3D-model build scripts and tests. Framework: React 19, built with Vite, installable offline PWA (vite-plugin-pwa), hosted on GitHub Pages. No backend: all data stays on the device (localStorage). Libraries: Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn/ui with Radix UI (components), Motion (animations), Lucide (icons), three.js with React Three Fiber and drei (3D body), WebLLM and Transformers.js (on-device AI for TOT). 3D models from the HuBMAP Human Reference Atlas and BodyParts3D (CC BY 4.0). Fonts: Oxanium, Space Grotesk, JetBrains Mono (SIL OFL).

TOT ASSISTANT

TOT is an AI assistant that runs entirely on the user’s device, offline, after a one-time model download. It uses open language models in the browser: Llama 3.2 1B (default on computers and tablets) or Qwen 2.5 0.5B / 1.5B, via WebLLM on WebGPU. On phones without WebGPU it uses SmolLM2 360M via Transformers.js on the processor. For each question, TOT gets the astronaut’s data as calculated by Khonsu (statuses, trends, radiation dose) and the matching passages from a small built-in science library with sources (retrieval). The model must use only this data, never invent numbers, and never diagnose. On the smallest models, Khonsu writes the measured values and “what to do” itself, and the AI only adds a short explanation. If the AI’s text contains numbers, it is dropped and a library sentence is shown instead, labelled “Background (library)”. Every answer lists its sources. A “Basic summary (not AI)” button gives a rule-based summary without any model. Nothing is sent anywhere.
